title: Counting objects to 20
keyIdea: Count each object once, say the number names in order, and stop at the target. The last number you say is how many objects there are — even when you count past ten into the teens.
familyTip: Put out a handful of spoons (about 12–18). Ask your child to tap each once and stop at a number you choose. Then spread the same spoons farther apart and ask: 'Still the same number?'

visual.caption: Careful counting — fair idea or myth? Drag each clue, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: last number said is how many
tap some objects twice to be sure
stop when you reach the target
moving objects always changes the total
sixteen is ten and six ones

lab.caption: Flagship lab: tap objects to a target, catch double-counts, keep the total after a rearrange, build a teen, then challenge.

kid: Tap each object once. Say one number for each tap.
The last number you say is how many are there.
Stop when you reach the target. Do not keep tapping.
Teens are ten and some ones. Sixteen is ten and six.
adult: EYFS / Y1 counting and cardinality (NC Number; CCSS K.CC): count objects to 20, one-to-one correspondence, cardinal principle, conservation when rearranged, teen structure as ten-and-ones.
Common mistakes: double-counting, skipping an object or a number name, thinking a spread-out group is 'more', treating teens as separate from tens and ones.
In the lab your child fills a mat to a target, fixes a double-count, checks that 14 stays 14 after a move, builds 16 from 10, then tries challenge traps for those slips.

practice.prompt: The last number you say tells you…
practice.hint: Finish a count of cups on the table and look at the final number word.
practice.explain: The cardinal principle: the last number names the total.

practice.prompt: Double-counting an object makes the total…
practice.hint: If you tap one spoon twice in a count of ten, what happens to the total?
practice.explain: An extra tap adds one to the spoken total, so it is too big.

practice.prompt: You count {n} buttons, tapping each once. How many buttons are there?
practice.hint: The count you finished is the total.
practice.explain: A fair one-to-one count ends on {n}, so there are {n} buttons.

practice.prompt: A mat has {n} counters. You add {k} more. How many now?
practice.hint: Add the new counters to the starting number.

practice.prompt: Order these counts from smallest to largest.
practice.hint: Compare the ones after the ten.
practice.explain: Compare the ones after the ten: 12, then 16, then 19.

pool.prompt: You move 14 counters farther apart. The number is…
pool.hint: Nothing was added or taken away.
pool.explain: Conservation: rearranging does not change how many.

pool.hint: Teens are built from a ten and some ones.
pool.explain: Seventeen means one ten and seven ones (10 + 7).

pool.prompt: When the target is 20 you should…
pool.explain: Stop when the last number matches the target.

pool.prompt: A skip in the count makes the total…
pool.hint: Missing an object leaves one out of the spoken total.

pool.prompt: You fairly counted {n} shells. How many shells?
pool.hint: The fair count is the total.
pool.explain: A fair one-to-one count ends on {n}, so there are {n} shells.

pool.prompt: A tray shows {n} cubes. You take away {k}. How many left?
Why tap each object only once?
choices: so the last number matches how many
pool.hint: One tap ↔ one object keeps the total honest.
pool.explain: One-to-one counting keeps the cardinal total correct.

pool.hint: Hear 'six-teen' as six with a ten.
pool.explain: Sixteen means one ten and six ones (10 + 6).
